facts.claim: The OurVinyl Sessions version of "Dark Black Coal" is track 2 on the four-song EP "Logan Halstead | OurVinyl Sessions", released June 7, 2022, and runs 3:27.
The EP is copyrighted 2022 OurVinyl TV, Inc.
Logan Halstead is credited as the writer of "Dark Black Coal (OurVinyl Sessions)".
A OurVinyl Sessions performance by Halstead was filmed and recorded live. The Facebook post says this about "Kentucky Sky" from the same session set.
Halstead wrote "Dark Black Coal" at age 15. He released a cellphone video of it in 2020.
RadioWV recorded and posted a video of "Dark Black Coal" in December 2020, and the video went viral. Halstead recorded it and "Far From Here" on the same day.
Halstead said the song is about the sacrifices his family and many others made for coal. He also said his dad, uncle, papaw and most of the men in his family worked in the mines around Boone County.
Halstead said he never thought of being a musician before the RadioWV video of "Dark Black Coal" took off, and that music had been a hobby.

The studio version of "Dark Black Coal" is the title track of Halstead's 2023 debut album on Thirty Tigers. Lawrence Rothman produced the album, which was recorded at Sound Emporium Studios in Nashville.
Halstead was born in Kentucky and raised in Boone County, West Virginia. He has cited Tyler Childers and Sturgill Simpson as influences, along with Cole Chaney and Nicholas Jamerson.

research.lineage: It sits in the Appalachian country-folk and Americana tradition of Kentucky and West Virginia singer-songwriters such as Tyler Childers, Sturgill Simpson and Cole Chaney, with coal-country storytelling.

draft:
The chorus of **Dark Black Coal** is a bargain, and the speaker isn't asking to win it. "Dark black coal, take my soul / I owe it to you anyways." There's no protest in that line. The mine already has him, and the debt is just stated as fact. What he asks for comes next, and it's smaller and more desperate: keep the mountain away from his children. Faith, resignation, and a father's fear are packed into four lines, and none of them cancels the others out.

Logan Halstead wrote it at 15. He has said the song is about the sacrifices his family and many others made for coal, and that his dad, his uncle, his papaw and most of the men in his family worked the mines around Boone County, West Virginia. That changes how the verses land. A teenager is describing the life the men around him lived, and the one waiting for him if the "boy with a hunger / To get far away from this town" never gets out.

Watch the pronouns. The verses keep saying "you": you wake up, you grab your hard hat, you pray you make it home. It's a way of describing pain at arm's length, the way people talk about their own lives when "I" is too much. Then the chorus drops the distance and says "my soul" and "my children." The second verse jumps "20 years older," and the hunger to leave is gone. In its place is a row of men underground, "Proving their collars are blue." That line holds pride and a kind of defensiveness at once. It's an identity worth claiming and also a life that keeps asking to be justified.

This OurVinyl Sessions take keeps it bare. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls through its arpeggios at an unhurried pace, and Halstead sings over it in a slightly raw, unvarnished voice with no harmonies and nothing to soften the room. The recording is close and dry, so the words carry all the weight. Halstead never leans on the grief. He states it plainly, the way people talk about loss they've grown up around.

The song first spread in 2020, through a cellphone video and then a RadioWV performance that went viral. Halstead has said he never thought of being a musician before it took off. A studio version became the title track of his 2023 Thirty Tigers debut. It belongs with the Kentucky and West Virginia writers he cites, Tyler Childers, Sturgill Simpson, Cole Chaney and Nicholas Jamerson, part of a coal-country tradition where the ballad is how a family's labor gets put on the record.

It sticks because the speaker has already given up on saving himself, so you end up carrying his one remaining hope for the kids.

factCheck.claim: Chorus quote: "Dark black coal, take my soul / I owe it to you anyways."
factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics exactly, and it's two consecutive lines.

factCheck.claim: The chorus asks to keep the mountain away from his children, and it is four lines long.
factCheck.note: Matches "Just don't let my children become the victims / Of the mountain's evil ways." The chorus is four lines.

factCheck.claim: Faith, resignation, and a father's fear are packed into the four chorus lines.
factCheck.note: The chorus has no prayer or faith language. The prayer is in an earlier verse. Replaced "faith" with "debt" so the reading rests on the chorus text.
